# Trajectory Learning Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts II through IV built closure around a fixed model. @Sec-vol3-evaluation ended Part IV by measuring task acceptance and comparing configurations, then testing explanations for failures under declared conditions. Part V changes the model itself. Training changes the proposals the runtime receives. It moves none of the H·S·A exposures, grants no authority, and removes none of the runtime's enforcement obligations. A changed policy can still alter the realized trajectory length, state use, and requested effects, so its behavior needs evaluation under those same contracts. The intervention ladder of @sec-vol3-flywheel-intervention-order places training after cheaper and more reversible changes to context, tools, and the runtime, as a default order that diagnostic evidence can shorten rather than a sequence every failure must climb. Curation decides which recorded trajectories support a particular learning use. Held-out evaluation and release policies then govern whether the resulting model may replace the one in service.

::: {#pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training .callout-principle title="Verified trajectory post-training"}

**Invariant**: A recorded outcome does not determine how a trajectory should be used for learning. Curation relates the evidence to a proposed behavior change, distinguishes admissible targets from contextual or rejected actions, and preserves the conditions under which the record was assessed. Recovery demonstrations expose decisions after errors that an error-free corpus does not cover; their value still depends on the intended tasks and learning objective. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-flywheel-gap and @sec-vol3-flywheel-curation.

**Implication**: A curation pipeline compares training with other system interventions, declares the consumer of each admitted record, and selects coverage and targets under a versioned data contract. Passing a task check does not automatically make every action in its trace a suitable demonstration.

:::

Once a trajectory is admitted, the imitation objective must distinguish the responses selected for learning from the context that supports them.

::: {#pri-vol3-action-masked-loss .callout-principle title="Observation loss masking"}

**Invariant**: For policy-response imitation, delivered observations condition the selected responses but are not themselves response targets. Predicting observation tokens adds a different objective; it does not turn generated text into authentic tool evidence. Context tokens can still affect gradients through the predictions that depend on them. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-masking.

**Implication**: Construct the loss mask from the admitted target spans and the actual serialized input, not from authorship alone. Preserve necessary conditioning information, specify how turn endings and incomplete responses are treated, and evaluate the resulting policy under the intended serving format. Masking changes supervision; the runtime still controls tool execution and evidence delivery.

:::

Imitation learns from selected responses, while preference learning compares assessed alternatives. Reinforcement learning instead collects new interactions and uses their rewards to guide policy updates.

::: {#pri-vol3-verifiable-rewards .callout-principle title="Reinforcement learning against isolated verifiers"}

**Invariant**: Reward-based optimization favors behavior according to the implemented score, which may differ from the task's requirements. Protecting the assessment mechanism prevents specific manipulation paths; it does not make an incomplete check a complete specification. The learning signal also depends on the estimator and sampled outcomes. Equal rewards eliminate the reward-driven term in the chapter's group-relative surrogate, not every possible learning signal. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-rlvr-need and @sec-vol3-rlvr-sandboxing.

**Implication**: An RL pipeline separates candidate-controlled material from assessment authority, contains candidate execution, and records the sampling and reward conditions used by each update. It tests whether the available exploration produces useful signal and evaluates the candidate on protected tasks under its intended runtime. Supervised initialization is one option, not a prerequisite imposed by reinforcement learning itself.

:::

The three chapters build from evidence selection to policy updates without prescribing a mandatory sequence of training methods. @Sec-vol3-trajectory-curation establishes which records and fixtures support a declared learning use. @Sec-vol3-fine-tuning turns admitted material into selected prediction targets or justified preference comparisons and an identified candidate policy. @Sec-vol3-rlvr adds fresh reward-scored interactions, explaining how their signal and execution cost shape the update. Verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) motivates checking candidates when assessment is more tractable than constructing a solution, but each check still needs a justified scope and resource budget. Changed weights can alter behavior, not grant authority. Part VI uses a measured single-agent configuration as the baseline for deciding whether coordination is worth its cost.
